source: MAFF Department of Agricultural Extension / Directorate General of Agriculture, "បច្ចេកទេសដាំដុះសណ្តែកសៀង" [Soybean cultivation techniques], official extension manual, 2018
text:
Pest section profiles the main insect pests farmers will encounter, each with photo-based identification and a short biology note plus control recommendations:

- Armyworm (Spodoptera spp.), Lepidoptera: eggs laid in masses on the underside of leaves covered in fuzzy scale, larvae feed on leaves and can cause severe defoliation in outbreak conditions; egg stage lasts roughly 4–5 days, larval stage roughly 20–26 days (varies by source condition), pupal stage in soil roughly 8–11 days. Recommended insecticides include Abamectin, Chlorpyrifos, Cypermethrin, Deltamethrin, alpha-cypermethrin, indoxacarb, flubendiamide, chlorantraniliprole, and Bacillus thuringiensis subsp. products, applied in rotation to avoid resistance buildup.
- Black cutworm (Agrotis ipsilon), Lepidoptera: nocturnal moth, larvae hide in soil by day and cut young seedlings at the base at night; egg stage roughly 2–4 days, larval stage roughly 18–40 days depending on temperature, pupates in soil.
- Pod borer (Maruca testulalis), Lepidoptera: larvae bore into flowers and young pods, feeding inside and causing flower/pod drop; control recommendations for the pod borer and related caterpillar pests include field sanitation (removing crop residue and volunteer host plants), proper spacing to reduce humidity, timely weeding, careful/measured insecticide use, and named products including Flubendiamide, chlorantraniliprole, Fipronil, indoxacarb, Bacillus thuringiensis, Emamectin benzoate, and permethrin.
- Bean bug (Riptortus linearis), Hemiptera, family Coreidae: adults and nymphs pierce and suck sap from pods, causing shrivelled or discolored seed; egg stage roughly 5–7 days, nymphs roughly 2 months to maturity, adults can live roughly 3–4 months and lay eggs continuously, making sustained field monitoring important.
- Stink bug (Nezara viridula, referred to in the source as "MilK bug"), Hemiptera, family Pentatomidae: similar pod-feeding damage to the bean bug, egg stage roughly 2–3 days, nymphal development roughly 15–30 days to adult, adults live roughly 23–33 days and can lay repeated egg batches.
- Green peach aphid (Myzus persicea), Homoptera, family Aphididae: colonies form on young shoots, leaf undersides, and flower buds, feeding on sap and causing curling/yellowing; the manual notes this species also vectors plant viruses, so aphid control is tied into the earlier bean-yellow-mosaic-virus vector-management advice.
- Bean thrips (Megalurothrips sitatus), Thysanoptera, family Thripidae: tiny insects feeding by rasping flower and leaf tissue, causing silvering/scarring and flower abortion under heavy pressure; population can build quickly under warm dry conditions.
- Bean leafhopper (Empoasea biguttula), Homoptera, family Cicadellidae: feeds on leaf sap causing yellowing and leaf-curl symptoms that can resemble nutrient deficiency; egg stage roughly 6–7 days, nymphal stage short, and multiple generations occur per season.
- Bruchid weevil (Callosobruchus chinensis), Coleoptera, family Bruchidae: a storage pest — adults lay eggs on pods in the field or on stored seed, and larvae bore into and develop inside individual seeds, causing weight loss and reduced seed viability/germination in storage.

Across these pest entries the manual repeats a consistent IPM-style control checklist: use healthy/clean seed, plant at recommended spacing, weed on time, avoid excess nitrogen (which can favor sap-feeding pest buildup), remove and destroy crop residue after harvest, and plant on a well-timed schedule to avoid peak pest pressure windows.
